stem: Which statement about magnetic field lines is correct?
options: They form closed loops and never cross one another
Outside a bar magnet they run from the S pole to the N pole
The field is strongest where the lines are farthest apart
They begin on north poles and end on south poles
explanation: Magnetic field lines are closed loops: outside a magnet they run from N to S and inside from S to N, so they have no start or end points. They cannot cross because the field has only one direction at each point. Lines that are closer together mean a stronger field, not a weaker one.

stem: The tesla (T), the SI unit of magnetic flux density, is equivalent to which combination of units?
explanation: From F = BIL, B = F/(IL), so 1 T = 1 N/(A·m). N·A/m and A·m/N rearrange the formula wrongly. N/(C·m) is missing the time unit: from F = qvB, 1 T = 1 N·s/(C·m).

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A long straight wire lies along the y axis and carries a current in the +y direction. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point on the +x axis, to the right of the wire?
options: Toward the top of the page (+y)
explanation: Grip the wire with the right thumb along +y; the fingers curl into the page on the right-hand side of the wire and out of the page on the left. The field of a straight wire circles the wire, so it can never point along the wire (+y) or radially away from it (+x). Out of the page is the field on the left side.

stem: A straight wire 0.5 m long carries a current of 4 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What is the magnitude of the force on the wire?
explanation: F = BIL = 0.2 × 4 × 0.5 = 0.4 N. Leaving out the length gives BI = 0.8 N. Dividing instead of multiplying, for example B/(IL) = 0.1, has the wrong units.

stem: A straight wire 0.2 m long carries a current of 5 A in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. The wire makes an angle of 30° with the field direction. What is the magnitude of the force on the wire?
explanation: F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wire and the field: F = 0.4 × 5 × 0.2 × sin 30° = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 N. Using cos 30° gives 0.2√3 N, and ignoring the angle gives 0.4 N.

stem: A straight wire carrying a current of 3 A lies parallel to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is the magnetic force on a 2 m length of the wire?
explanation: F = BIL sin θ and θ = 0° when the wire is parallel to the field, so sin θ = 0 and the force is zero. The value 3 N is BIL, which applies only when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A uniform magnetic field points into the page. A straight wire in the page carries a current in the +x direction. In which direction is the magnetic force on the wire?
options: Toward the bottom of the page (−y)
Toward the top of the page (+y)
explanation: F = IL × B with L along +x and B along −z: x̂ × (−ẑ) = +ŷ, so the force points toward the top of the page. The force is always perpendicular to both the wire and the field, so it cannot be out of the page or along −x. Getting −y comes from taking the field out of the page.

stem: A proton (charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 2 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it?
explanation: F = qvB = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁶ × 0.5 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. Forgetting B gives qv = 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ N, and dividing by B instead of multiplying gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹³ N.

stem: A charged particle moves in a region that contains only a uniform magnetic field. Which quantity of the particle stays constant?
explanation: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the kinetic energy, and hence the speed, stays constant. The direction of motion changes, so velocity, momentum and the (centripetal) acceleration vector all change.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. An electron moves in the +x direction through a uniform magnetic field that points out of the page. In which direction is the magnetic force on the electron?
options: Toward the bottom of the page
Toward the top of the page
explanation: F = qv × B. For a positive charge, x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ (toward the bottom). The electron is negative, so the force is reversed: toward the top of the page. Choosing the bottom of the page forgets the negative charge; the force cannot be along the field (out of or into the page).

stem: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 4 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What is the radius of its circular path?
explanation: qvB = mv²/r gives r = mv/(qB) = (1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ × 4 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.2) = 6.4 × 10⁻²¹/3.2 × 10⁻²⁰ = 0.2 m. Mishandling the factor 0.2 in the denominator (dividing by 2 instead of 0.2, or by 0.1) gives 0.02 m-type or 0.4 m answers.

stem: A charged particle moves in a circle perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled (field unchanged), what happens to the period of its circular motion?
explanation: r = mv/(qB), so doubling v doubles r; the period T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on speed. The particle travels a circle twice as long at twice the speed, so the time per revolution is unchanged. 'It halves' ignores the larger radius.

stem: A proton and an alpha particle (mass 4 times and charge 2 times that of the proton) enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same speed, perpendicular to the field. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to that of the proton?
explanation: r = mv/(qB), so r is proportional to m/q at equal speeds. For the alpha particle m/q = 4/2 = 2 times the proton's, so its radius is 2 times larger. Using mass alone gives 4 and forgetting that the charge is in the denominator gives 1/2.

stem: A proton and an alpha particle (mass 4 times and charge 2 times that of the proton) enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same kinetic energy, perpendicular to the field. What is the ratio of their radii, r(proton) : r(alpha)?
explanation: With momentum p = √(2mEk), r = p/(qB) = √(2mEk)/(qB). For the alpha particle √m is 2 times and q is 2 times the proton's, so the two factors cancel and the radii are equal. The ratio 1 : 2 is the result for equal speeds, not equal kinetic energies.

stem: A proton and a deuteron (same charge, twice the mass of the proton) start from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference and then enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it. What is the ratio of their radii, r(proton) : r(deuteron)?
explanation: qU = ½mv² gives v = √(2qU/m), so r = mv/(qB) = √(2mU/q)/B, which is proportional to √(m/q). The deuteron has twice the mass and the same charge, so its radius is √2 times the proton's: 1 : √2. The ratio 1 : 2 would apply at equal speeds.

stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. Using B = μ₀I/(2πr) with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, what is the magnetic flux density at a distance of 2 cm from the wire?
explanation: B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 0.02) = (2 × 10⁻⁶)/0.02 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T. Leaving out the 2π gives 2π × 10⁻⁴ T, and using π instead of 2π gives 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ T. Taking 2 cm as 0.2 m gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ T.

stem: The magnetic flux density at 3 cm from a long straight current-carrying wire is 6 μT. What is it at 9 cm from the same wire?
explanation: For a long straight wire B = μ₀I/(2πr), so B is inversely proportional to r. Tripling the distance divides B by 3: 6/3 = 2 μT. Treating it as an inverse-square law gives 6/9 ≈ 0.67 μT, and 18 μT has B increasing with distance.

stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. Which statement is correct?
options: They exert no force on each other
Only the wire with the larger current feels a force
explanation: Each wire sits in the field of the other, and applying F = IL × B shows the force on each points toward the other wire: parallel currents attract. By Newton's third law both wires feel equal and opposite forces, so it is not only one wire. Repulsion happens for opposite currents.

stem: Two long parallel wires 0.1 m apart each carry 5 A, in opposite directions. Use B = μ₀I/(2πr) with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What is the force on a 2 m length of one wire, and is it attractive or repulsive?
explanation: The field of one wire at the other is B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5/0.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁵ T, so F = BIL = 1 × 10⁻⁵ × 5 × 2 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ N. Opposite currents repel. The value 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ N is the force per metre, not on 2 m.

stem: A solenoid lies along the x axis. Seen from a point on the +x axis looking toward the solenoid, the current in the turns flows anticlockwise. Which end is the north pole, and in which direction does the field inside point?
options: +x end; the field inside points along −x
−x end; the field inside points along +x
−x end; the field inside points along −x
+x end; the field inside points along +x
explanation: With the right-hand grip rule, fingers along the anticlockwise current as seen from +x give a thumb pointing toward the viewer, along +x. Inside a solenoid the field runs from the S end to the N end, so the field inside points along +x and the +x end is the north pole. A field inside pointing toward the north end is consistent; the field points from N to S only outside.

stem: The north pole of a compass needle points toward the Earth's geographic North Pole. What does this show about the Earth's magnetic field?
options: A magnetic north pole lies near the geographic North Pole
The Earth's field lines point from north to south at the surface
A magnetic south pole lies near the geographic North Pole
The Earth's field is strongest at the equator
explanation: Unlike poles attract, so the needle's N pole is pulled toward a magnetic south pole, which lies near the geographic North Pole. Consequently the Earth's field lines at the surface point roughly from south to north. The field is strongest near the poles, not at the equator.

stem: A horizontal metal rod of mass 0.02 kg and length 0.4 m lies in a horizontal uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T perpendicular to the rod. What current makes the magnetic force on the rod exactly balance its weight? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: BIL = mg gives I = mg/(BL) = (0.02 × 10)/(0.5 × 0.4) = 0.2/0.2 = 1 A. Using the mass 0.02 kg instead of the weight 0.2 N gives 0.1 A, and forgetting the length gives 0.2/0.5 = 0.4 A.

stem: A horizontal rod of mass 0.05 kg and length 0.5 m hangs from two light vertical threads. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.2 T is switched on and a current of 5 A flows through the rod. At equilibrium, what angle do the threads make with the vertical? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: The magnetic force is horizontal: F = BIL = 0.2 × 5 × 0.5 = 0.5 N, and the weight is mg = 0.5 N. The thread tension balances both, so tan θ = F/(mg) = 1 and θ = 45°. The threads cannot reach 90° because the weight always has to be supported.

stem: A square coil of 50 turns, each 10 cm × 10 cm, carries a current of 2 A in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What is the maximum torque on the coil?
explanation: The maximum torque, when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, is τ = NBIA = 50 × 0.2 × 2 × 0.01 = 0.2 N·m. Forgetting the 50 turns gives 0.004 N·m, and taking the area as 0.1 m² instead of (0.1 m)² = 0.01 m² gives 2 N·m.

stem: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field of 2 × 10⁴ V/m and a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T are perpendicular to each other and to the ion beam. At what speed do ions pass straight through?
explanation: No deflection when qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2 × 10⁴/0.1 = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s, whatever the charge or mass. B/E gives 5 × 10⁻⁶ m/s and E × B gives 2.0 × 10³ m/s, neither of which balances the forces.

stem: In a velocity selector, a uniform electric field E and a uniform magnetic field B are perpendicular to each other and to the beam. Which statement is correct?
options: Only positive ions with speed E/B pass undeflected
Ions faster than E/B are deflected in the direction of the electric force
An electron with speed E/B also passes undeflected
Ions with speed E/B pass undeflected only if their mass is small
explanation: The condition qE = qvB gives v = E/B, which contains neither the charge, its sign, nor the mass. For an electron both forces reverse together, so they still cancel. A faster ion feels a larger magnetic force qvB > qE, so it is deflected toward the magnetic force, not the electric force.

stem: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T. What is the period of its motion?
explanation: T = 2πm/(qB) = 2π × (1.6 × 10⁻²⁷)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) = 2π × 10⁻⁸/0.1 = 2π × 10⁻⁷ s. Forgetting to divide by B gives 2π × 10⁻⁸ s, multiplying by B gives 2π × 10⁻⁹ s, and π × 10⁻⁷ s is only half a revolution.

stem: The region between the lines x = 0 and x = d contains a uniform magnetic field into the page; elsewhere there is no field. A charged particle enters at x = 0 moving in the +x direction, perpendicular to the boundary. The radius of its circular path in the field is 2d. Through what angle is its direction of motion turned when it leaves the region at x = d?
explanation: The centre of the circle lies on the line x = 0, a distance r = 2d from the entry point. When the particle reaches x = d, the radius to it makes angle θ with the boundary line where sin θ = d/r = 1/2, so θ = 30°, and the velocity turns through the same angle. 60° comes from using cos θ = 1/2, and 90° would require r = d.

stem: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged ions (charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 3.2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) start from rest, are accelerated through 1000 V, and enter a uniform 0.2 T field perpendicular to its boundary. They travel a semicircle and hit a detector on the boundary. How far from the entry point do they hit?
explanation: qU = ½mv² gives v² = 2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000/3.2 × 10⁻²⁶ = 10¹⁰, so v = 10⁵ m/s. Then r = mv/(qB) = 3.2 × 10⁻²¹/3.2 × 10⁻²⁰ = 0.1 m. After a semicircle the ion lands one diameter away, 2r = 0.2 m; 0.1 m is only the radius.

stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field moving exactly parallel to the field lines. What is the shape of its path in the field?
explanation: The magnetic force is qvB sin θ, and θ = 0 for motion along the field, so there is no force and the electron keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed. A circle needs velocity perpendicular to B, and a helix needs a velocity component both along and across the field.

stem: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a uniform 0.1 T magnetic field with speed 2 × 10⁶ m/s at 60° to the field direction. What is the radius of the resulting helical path?
explanation: Only the velocity component perpendicular to B causes circular motion: v⊥ = v sin 60° = √3 × 10⁶ m/s. Then r = mv⊥/(qB) = 10⁻⁸ × √3 × 10⁶/0.1 = 0.1√3 m. Using the parallel component (10⁶ m/s) gives 0.1 m, and using the full speed gives 0.2 m.

stem: Which of the following produces a magnetic field?
options: A charged metal sphere at rest
A steady current in a copper wire
A charged plastic rod held still
explanation: Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges, so a steady current in a wire (Oersted's discovery) creates one. Charges at rest, such as a charged sphere, a stationary electron or a charged rod, produce only electric fields.

stem: A circular loop of wire lies in the plane of the page and carries a current that flows clockwise as seen by the reader. What is the direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the loop?
options: Toward the top of the page, in the plane of the loop
The field at the centre is zero
explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand clockwise along the current: the thumb points into the page, which is the field direction at the centre. Every part of the loop contributes a field into the page at the centre, so the contributions add rather than cancel. Out of the page would correspond to an anticlockwise current.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A long straight wire passes through the origin perpendicular to the page, with current flowing out of the page. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point on the +y axis, above the wire?
explanation: With the thumb out of the page, the fingers curl anticlockwise as seen by the reader. At the top of such a circle the anticlockwise direction points to the left, −x. The field is tangent to the circle, so it cannot point along ±y (radially). +x is the result for a current into the page.

stem: Two long straight wires perpendicular to the page pass through x = −2 cm and x = +2 cm on the x axis (+x to the right, +y toward the top of the page). Each carries 4 A: the left one out of the page, the right one into the page. Using B = μ₀I/(2πr) with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, what is the field at the origin?
explanation: Each wire gives B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 4/0.02 = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T at the origin. The left wire (out of the page) gives an anticlockwise field, which points along +y to its right; the right wire (into the page) gives a clockwise field, which points along +y to its left. The two add to 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ T along +y; they would cancel only if the currents were in the same direction.

stem: Two long parallel wires exert a force F on each other. Both currents are doubled and the distance between the wires is also doubled. What is the new force between them?
explanation: The force per unit length is μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd), proportional to I₁I₂/d. Doubling both currents multiplies the force by 4, and doubling d divides it by 2, so the new force is 2F. 4F forgets the change in distance.

stem: How is the direction of the magnetic field at a point defined?
options: The direction in which the N pole of a small compass needle points
The direction of the force on a positive charge moving through the point
The direction from the nearest S pole toward the nearest N pole
The direction of the force on a current-carrying wire at the point
explanation: By definition the field direction is the direction in which the north pole of a small compass needle at that point points. The magnetic force on a moving charge or on a wire is perpendicular to the field, not along it. Outside a magnet the field runs from N to S, not from S to N.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A beam of electrons travels in the +x direction and is bent toward the top of the page by a uniform magnetic field. What is the direction of the field?
explanation: For the electron F = −e(v × B) must be +ŷ, so v × B must be −ŷ. With v along +x, x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ, so B points out of the page (+z). Into the page would bend a positive charge upward but an electron downward. A field along ±y would push the beam into or out of the page.

stem: A rectangular loop 0.2 m × 0.1 m lies in the plane of the page and carries a current of 2 A. A uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T points into the page. What is the magnitude of the net magnetic force on the loop?
explanation: The forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite: each long side feels BIL = 0.5 × 2 × 0.2 = 0.2 N and each short side 0.1 N, in opposite directions. In a uniform field the net force on any closed current loop is zero. Adding the magnitudes gives 0.6 N, which ignores the directions.

stem: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a uniform 0.2 T magnetic field perpendicular to its boundary and to the field, travels a semicircle and leaves. How long does it spend in the field?
explanation: The full period is T = 2πm/(qB) = 2π × 10⁻⁸/0.2 = π × 10⁻⁷ s. A semicircle takes half a period, 5π × 10⁻⁸ s. π × 10⁻⁷ s is the full period, and 2.5π × 10⁻⁸ s is a quarter of it.

stem: An alpha particle (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 5 × 10⁵ m/s in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. Its velocity makes an angle of 30° with the field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it?
explanation: F = qvB sin θ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10⁵ × 0.4 × 0.5 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Ignoring the angle gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, and using cos 30° gives 3.2√3 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.

stem: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle of radius 0.1 m in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is its speed?
explanation: r = mv/(qB) gives v = qBr/m = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.5 × 0.1)/(1.6 × 10⁻²⁷) = 10⁸ × 0.05 = 5 × 10⁶ m/s. Dividing by B instead of multiplying gives 2 × 10⁷ m/s, and the other values come from power-of-ten slips.

stem: An electron and a proton enter the same uniform magnetic field with momenta of equal magnitude, both perpendicular to the field. Which statement is correct?
options: They move on circles of equal radius in the same sense
The electron's circle is larger and they turn in opposite senses
They move on circles of equal radius in opposite senses
The proton's circle is larger and they turn in the same sense
explanation: r = mv/(qB) = p/(qB); the momenta are equal and the charges have equal magnitude, so the radii are equal. The charges have opposite signs, so the forces at the same velocity are opposite and the particles circulate in opposite senses. Comparing masses alone would apply at equal speeds, not equal momenta.

stem: A proton moves in the plane of the page in a uniform magnetic field pointing into the page. How does it circulate, as seen by the reader?
options: It moves in a straight line
explanation: Take v along +x and B along −z: F = qv × B = q(x̂ × (−ẑ)) = +ŷ. A particle moving right and pushed toward the top of the page turns left, which is anticlockwise. Clockwise motion is what an electron would do, and since v is perpendicular to B there is no motion along the field.

stem: Ions of one kind start from rest, are accelerated through a voltage U and then move in a circle of radius r in a fixed magnetic field. What accelerating voltage makes the radius 2r?
explanation: qU = ½mv² gives v ∝ √U, and r = mv/(qB) ∝ v, so r ∝ √U. Doubling r needs √U to double, so U must become 4U. 2U would only increase the radius by a factor √2.

stem: A flat metal strip lies in the plane of the page (+x to the right, +y toward the top of the page). A current flows in the +x direction and is carried by electrons. A uniform magnetic field points out of the page. Which edge of the strip reaches the higher potential?
options: Neither: there is no potential difference across the strip
explanation: The electrons move in the −x direction. For them F = −e(v × B) with v × B = (−x̂) × ẑ = +ŷ, so the force is −ŷ and electrons collect on the bottom edge, making it negative; the top edge is at the higher potential. Positive carriers moving along +x would also be pushed to the bottom edge but would make it the higher one, which is why choosing the bottom edge is the trap.

stem: A wire is bent into a semicircle of radius 0.1 m. It lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T and carries a current of 2 A. What is the magnitude of the net force on the semicircular wire?
explanation: In a uniform field a curved wire feels the same net force as a straight wire joining its ends; here that is the diameter, 0.2 m. F = BIL = 0.5 × 2 × 0.2 = 0.2 N. Using the arc length π × 0.1 m gives 0.1π N, which ignores that the forces on different parts point in different directions; using the radius gives 0.1 N.

stem: An electron moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. The field strength is doubled while the speed stays the same. Which statement is correct?
options: The radius halves and the period halves
The radius halves and the period is unchanged
The radius doubles and the period halves
The radius is unchanged and the period halves
explanation: r = mv/(qB) and T = 2πm/(qB) are both inversely proportional to B, so doubling B halves both. The period does not depend on speed, but it does depend on B, which is why 'period unchanged' is wrong.

stem: Which statement about the magnetic field of a bar magnet is correct?
options: Inside the magnet the field lines run from N to S
The field is zero inside the magnet
The field lines end at the poles
Inside the magnet the field lines run from S to N
explanation: Field lines are closed loops: outside the magnet they run from N to S and they continue inside the magnet from S back to N. They do not end at the poles and the field inside is not zero. 'From N to S inside' would make the lines meet head-on at the poles.

stem: A circular loop of radius 0.1 m carries a current of 5 A. Using B = μ₀I/(2R) for the field at the centre, with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, what is the field at the centre?
explanation: B = μ₀I/(2R) = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 5)/(2 × 0.1) = 20π × 10⁻⁷/0.2 = π × 10⁻⁵ T. Leaving out the factor 2 gives 2π × 10⁻⁵ T, and using the straight-wire formula μ₀I/(2πR) gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ T.

stem: A compass needle rests in the Earth's horizontal magnetic field. A long vertical wire nearby is switched on; at the compass its field is horizontal, perpendicular to the Earth's horizontal field and of the same magnitude. Through what angle does the needle turn?
explanation: The needle aligns with the resultant of two perpendicular horizontal fields of equal size B. The angle θ from the original direction satisfies tan θ = B/B = 1, so θ = 45°. It would turn through 90° only if the Earth's field were absent.

stem: Positive ions pass undeflected through a region with a uniform electric field E perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B. When the electric field is switched off, the ions move on a circle of radius r. What is their charge-to-mass ratio q/m?
explanation: Undeflected motion gives qE = qvB, so v = E/B. In the magnetic field alone r = mv/(qB) = mE/(qB²), so q/m = E/(B²r). The answer E/(Br) forgets that v itself contains a factor 1/B.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A straight wire lies along the y axis with current in the +y direction. A uniform magnetic field points in the +x direction. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
explanation: F = IL × B with L along +y and B along +x: ŷ × x̂ = −ẑ, so the force is into the page. The force must be perpendicular to both the wire and the field, which rules out ±x. Out of the page comes from reversing the order of the cross product.

stem: Four particles move with the same speed perpendicular to the same uniform magnetic field. Which one is NOT deflected?
explanation: The magnetic force is F = qvB, so only charged particles are deflected. The neutron has no charge and continues in a straight line; the proton, the electron and the alpha particle are all charged and move on circles.

stem: A metal rod of mass 0.1 kg rests across two smooth horizontal rails 0.5 m apart in a vertical uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. A current of 2 A flows through the rod. What is the initial acceleration of the rod?
explanation: The magnetic force is F = BIL = 0.4 × 2 × 0.5 = 0.4 N, horizontal and perpendicular to the rod. Then a = F/m = 0.4/0.1 = 4 m/s². The value 0.4 is the force in newtons, not the acceleration, and 8 m/s² forgets the factor 0.5 for the length.

stem: Two smooth parallel rails 0.4 m apart are inclined at 30° to the horizontal. A uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. A rod of mass 0.2 kg lies across the rails, perpendicular to them. What current through the rod keeps it at rest? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: With B perpendicular to the incline, the magnetic force BIL acts along the incline and must balance the component of weight down the slope: BIL = mg sin 30° = 2 × 0.5 = 1 N. So I = 1/(0.5 × 0.4) = 5 A. Using mg cos 30° gives 5√3 A, and using the full weight gives 10 A.

stem: A charged particle moves half way round a circle of radius 0.1 m in a uniform magnetic field; the magnetic force on it has constant magnitude 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. How much work does the magnetic force do on the particle?
explanation: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work over any path, and the kinetic energy stays the same. Multiplying the force by the arc length (π × 0.1 m) gives 2π × 10⁻¹⁵ J, which wrongly assumes the force is along the motion.

stem: Two long parallel wires 0.4 m apart carry currents of 2 A and 6 A in the same direction. At what point on the line joining them, between the wires, is the magnetic field zero?
options: There is no such point between the wires
explanation: Between wires with parallel currents the two fields point in opposite directions, so they cancel where μ₀I₁/(2πx) = μ₀I₂/(2π(0.4 − x)): 2/x = 6/(0.4 − x), giving 0.8 − 2x = 6x and x = 0.10 m. The zero point is nearer the smaller current. 0.30 m from the 2 A wire puts it nearer the larger current, and the midpoint would need equal currents.

stem: A flat circular coil lies in the plane of the page and carries a current that flows anticlockwise as seen by the reader. Which statement about the coil is correct?
options: The face toward the reader acts as a south pole
The face toward the reader acts as a north pole
Its field at the centre lies in the plane of the page
Its field at the centre points into the page
explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, an anticlockwise current gives a field out of the page at the centre, so field lines leave the face toward the reader, which therefore acts as a north pole. The field at the centre is perpendicular to the coil, not in its plane. A clockwise current would make the reader's face a south pole.

stem: Two kinds of singly charged ions enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same speed, perpendicular to it. They move on circles of radius 15 cm and 10 cm. The lighter ion has mass 2.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. What is the mass of the heavier ion?
explanation: r = mv/(qB) with equal q, v and B, so r is proportional to m. The lighter ion has the smaller radius (10 cm), so the heavier mass is 2.0 × 10⁻²⁶ × 15/10 = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Inverting the ratio gives 1.33 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, and squaring it gives 4.5 × 10⁻²⁶ kg.

stem: A straight wire 0.3 m long carrying 2 A lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is the force on the wire?
explanation: F = BIL = 0.5 × 2 × 0.3 = 0.3 N. Leaving out B gives IL = 0.6 N, and dividing by the length gives BI/L ≈ 3.3 N.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A straight wire in the page carries current in the +y direction through a uniform magnetic field pointing out of the page. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
explanation: F = IL × B with L along +y and B along +z: ŷ × ẑ = +x̂, so the force points to the right. The force is perpendicular to both wire and field, so it cannot be along the current or into the page. −x would be the answer for a field into the page.

stem: Which of the following is equivalent to 1 tesla in SI base units?
explanation: 1 T = 1 N/(A·m) and 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², so 1 T = 1 kg·m/(s²·A·m) = 1 kg/(A·s²). kg·m/(A·s²) forgets to cancel the metre, and kg/(A·s) has the wrong power of seconds.

stem: An electron (charge magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1 × 10⁷ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.01 T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it?
explanation: F = qvB = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁷ × 0.01 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Forgetting B gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹² N, and dividing by B gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ N.

stem: An alpha particle (mass 6.4 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is the radius of its path?
explanation: r = mv/(qB) = (6.4 × 10⁻²⁷ × 10⁶)/(3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.5) = 6.4 × 10⁻²¹/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.04 m. Using the proton charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C instead of 2e gives 0.08 m.

stem: Two protons move on circles in the same uniform magnetic field, one with twice the speed of the other. Which quantity is the same for both?
options: The magnitude of the magnetic force
explanation: T = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on speed, so both have the same period. The radius r = mv/(qB) and the force qvB are proportional to v, and the kinetic energy is proportional to v², so these all differ.

stem: A long straight wire carries 3 A. Using B = μ₀I/(2πr) with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, what is the field 6 cm from the wire?
explanation: B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 3/0.06 = 6 × 10⁻⁷/0.06 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Leaving out the 2π gives 2π × 10⁻⁵ T, and using π instead of 2π gives 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T.

stem: A long straight wire is perpendicular to the page with the current flowing into the page. How do the magnetic field lines around it look to the reader?
options: Straight lines pointing away from the wire
Anticlockwise circles centred on the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Clockwise circles centred on the wire
explanation: The field of a straight wire forms circles centred on the wire. Pointing the right thumb into the page, the fingers curl clockwise as seen by the reader. Anticlockwise circles would correspond to a current out of the page.

stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents of 2 A and 6 A in opposite directions. Which statement about the forces between them is correct?
options: The forces are equal in magnitude and repulsive
The forces are equal in magnitude and attractive
The 6 A wire feels three times the force; repulsive
The 2 A wire feels three times the force; attractive
explanation: The force per unit length on either wire is μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd), which contains both currents, so the forces are equal (as Newton's third law requires). Antiparallel currents repel. Thinking the larger current feels a larger force forgets that each wire's force depends on the other wire's field too.

stem: A velocity selector uses a magnetic field of 0.05 T. What electric field strength lets ions with speed 4 × 10⁵ m/s pass straight through?
explanation: qE = qvB gives E = vB = 4 × 10⁵ × 0.05 = 2 × 10⁴ V/m. Dividing v by B gives 8 × 10⁶ V/m, and B/v gives 1.25 × 10⁻⁷ V/m.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A positive ion moves into the page through a uniform magnetic field that points in the +x direction. What is the direction of the magnetic force on the ion?
explanation: F = qv × B with v along −z and B along +x: (−ẑ) × x̂ = −(ẑ × x̂) = −ŷ, so the force points toward the bottom of the page. +y results from dropping the minus sign of the velocity. The force cannot be along B (+x) or along the velocity.

stem: Two particles with equal charge and the same kinetic energy enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it. Their masses are in the ratio 1 : 4. What is the ratio of the radii of their paths?
explanation: r = mv/(qB) = √(2mEk)/(qB), so at equal charge and kinetic energy r is proportional to √m. The ratio is √1 : √4 = 1 : 2. The ratio 1 : 4 is what equal speeds would give.

stem: In which situation does a charged particle experience a magnetic force?
options: It is at rest in a magnetic field
It moves perpendicular to a magnetic field
It moves parallel to a magnetic field
It is an uncharged atom moving across a field
explanation: The magnetic force is F = qvB sin θ. It is zero when v = 0, when the motion is along the field (sin θ = 0) or when q = 0. Only a charge moving across the field, here perpendicular to it, feels a force.

stem: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top of the page. A horizontal rod of mass 0.03 kg and length 0.2 m lies along the x axis, hanging from two light threads, in a uniform 0.5 T field into the page. What current makes the thread tension zero? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: The magnetic force must point up (+y) and equal the weight: BIL = mg gives I = 0.3/(0.5 × 0.2) = 3 A. F = IL × B with B along −z gives +ŷ when L is along +x, since x̂ × (−ẑ) = +ŷ. A current along −x would push the rod down and increase the tension.

stem: A straight wire feels a force of 0.8 N when it is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The wire is turned, keeping the current the same, until it makes an angle of 30° with the field. What is the force now?
explanation: F = BIL sin θ, so the force is 0.8 × sin 30° = 0.4 N. Using cos 30° gives 0.4√3 N. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.

stem: In a mass spectrometer, two kinds of singly charged ions are accelerated from rest through the same voltage and then enter the same magnetic field. The radii of their paths are in the ratio 1 : 2. What is the ratio of their masses?
explanation: qU = ½mv² and r = mv/(qB) combine to r = √(2mU/q)/B, so r ∝ √m for equal charges and voltages. A radius ratio 1 : 2 means a mass ratio 1 : 4. The answer 1 : 2 treats r as proportional to m, which holds only for equal speeds.

stem: A uniform magnetic field fills a strip of width 0.05 m with straight parallel boundaries. Protons (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enter at 1 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to the boundary and to the field. What is the smallest field that stops them from crossing to the other side?
explanation: The protons just fail to cross when the radius of their path equals the width of the strip: r = mv/(qB) ≤ d gives B ≥ mv/(qd) = (1.6 × 10⁻²¹)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.05) = 0.01/0.05 = 0.2 T. Requiring the diameter to equal the width gives 0.1 T, which is too weak: those protons still cross.

stem: A flat circular coil of 100 turns and radius 0.1 m carries a current of 0.5 A. Using B = μ₀NI/(2R) with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, what is the field at the centre?
explanation: B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 100 × 0.5)/(2 × 0.1) = 20π × 10⁻⁶/0.2 = π × 10⁻⁴ T. Forgetting the 100 turns gives π × 10⁻⁶ T, leaving out the 2 gives 2π × 10⁻⁴ T, and using the straight-wire formula gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T.

stem: Which statement describes the magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire?
options: Straight lines parallel to the wire
Straight lines radiating out from the wire
Circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
Closed loops that pass through the wire from end to end
explanation: The field of a straight current forms concentric circles around the wire, in planes perpendicular to it, with the sense given by the right-hand grip rule. Radial lines describe the electric field of a line of charge, not a magnetic field.

stem: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its straight boundary and to the field. It travels a semicircle of radius r in time t and leaves. A second proton enters the same way with twice the speed. What are the radius and the time in the field for the second proton?
explanation: r = mv/(qB) doubles with speed, giving 2r. The time for a semicircle is half the period, πm/(qB), which does not depend on speed, so it is still t. 'Time 2t' forgets that the faster proton covers the longer path at twice the speed.
